title: Fraud Detection and Forensics
answer: Expense fraud, money laundering networks, vendor fraud, communication forensics and tracing digital assets.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Expense Fraud
children.blurb: Expense fraud covers duplicate claims, inflated amounts, personal costs submitted as business expenses, fictitious receipts, and collusion between employees and approvers or vendors.

children.name: Money Laundering Networks
children.blurb: Money laundering networks are groups of individuals, shell companies, accounts, and transactions arranged to move illicit funds while obscuring origin and ownership.

children.name: Phantom Vendors and Procurement Fraud
children.blurb: Phantom vendors are supplier records that exist only on paper or in a system, created to route payments to a fraudster rather than a real provider of goods or services.

children.name: Communication Forensics
children.blurb: Communication forensics applies analytical methods to emails, chat logs, call recordings, and other message data to uncover fraud, reconstruct events, and support investigations.

children.name: Tracing and Recovering Digital Assets
children.blurb: Tracing and recovering digital assets covers the identification, location, and legal recovery of funds or tokenized property that have been moved through cryptocurrency wallets, exchanges, decentralized finance protocols, and other digital channels.

sections.body: This field applies machine learning and pattern recognition to financial records, transaction logs, and communications. AI systems now flag expense claims that deviate from an employee's own history or from peer norms, and they score vendor invoices for signs of duplication or shell company traits. In money laundering work, models look for layered transfers, structuring just below reporting thresholds, and circular flows between related accounts. Communication forensics uses language models to compare writing style across emails, contracts, and chat logs, while tracing digital assets follows cryptocurrency movements across public ledgers. These are operational tools, not hypothetical ones, and they run inside banks, insurers, audit firms, and corporate finance teams.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The solved parts are narrow and well defined: expense fraud detection works reliably when there is enough labeled history, and duplicate invoice checks are mature. Money laundering network detection is less settled, because real networks are sparse, adaptive, and often hidden inside legitimate business activity. Phantom vendor detection still produces many false positives, especially for small suppliers with thin documentation. Communication forensics can match style but cannot prove intent or authorship to a legal standard on its own. Tracing digital assets is technically strong for transparent blockchains but weak when funds move through mixers, privacy coins, or uncooperative exchanges. The honest limit is that these systems narrow the search space and rank risk, they do not replace human investigation or regulatory judgment.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader looking at individual employee claims should start with Expense Fraud, which covers outlier detection, receipt analysis, and policy rule engines. Money Laundering Networks moves up a level to graph-based detection across accounts, jurisdictions, and time, and it explains why network structure matters more than single transactions. Phantom Vendors and Procurement Fraud sits between the two, focused on supplier identity, invoicing patterns, and conflicts of interest. Communication Forensics shifts from numbers to language, showing how stylometry and entity resolution connect people to documents. Tracing and Recovering Digital Assets closes the loop by following the money after fraud is suspected, across wallets, exchanges, and legal recovery routes. Together they move from individual misconduct to organized schemes and then to asset recovery.
